title: “我们都是在演即兴喜剧时认识的”——在洛杉矶这个全球开发成本最高的地方做喜剧游戏的独立工作室
content:
"We all met by doing improv comedy" – The Los Angeles indie studio making a comedy game in one of the most expensive places for game dev in the world | GamesIndustry.biz

.
What do you get if you cross a SpaceX engineer, a TV writer, and a former professor?
Give up?
The answer is Mad Herons, a new Los Angeles-based indie studio working on their comedy-focused debut title,
Send In The Clown
.
Technical and game design lead Nick Park was formerly an engineer at SpaceX and Nvidia, while creative and audio lead Jacques Mouledoux was a writer on the Paramount+ TV show iCarly, as well as a contributor to the satirical news site Hard Drive. Rounding out the co-founders is operations and strategic lead Karen Park, a veteran of the LA improv comedy scene who was previously a professor at the University of Pittsburgh.
The trio are aiming to draw on their diverse experiences and shared love of comedy to make a game about a clown saving a 12-year-old's disastrous birthday party – a game that makes a selling point of only being an hour long.
GamesIndustry.biz
asked the three studio founders what makes for a good comedy game, and how they're finding funding on America's expensive West Coast.
Relatively few games companies target comedy, which can be notoriously hard to do – what do you see as some of the most successful examples of comedy games, and why do they work?
Jacques Mouledoux  |
Image credit:
Mad Herons
Jacques Mouledoux
: Comedy is certainly hard, but there are so many hilarious games. My favourite game of all time is Portal, which is so funny, but I also love Untitled Goose Game, Disco Elysium, Earthbound, and so many more.
I think comedy games work best when they allow the players themselves to be funny. Disco Elysium, for instance, has the sort of hilarious situations and hilarious characters (shoutout Cuno) you might find in a comedy film or TV show, but the game goes further and allows you to make completely unhinged decisions; you feel like
you
are funny. And then you have something like Untitled Goose Game where you truly feel like an extremely obnoxious goose, because that's what you have to be in order to succeed at the game. What I'm saying is that I want to be unhinged and/or a goose.
Nick Park
: I'll echo Jacques in loving the Portal series and Untitled Goose Game, and will add Psychonauts as a personal favorite. I think one thing these games share is that their comedy isn't just a thin layer of one-liners on top of the gameplay or plot, but is woven throughout every element of the game. You can tell the creators thought about comedy first, and made sure their mechanics, level design, art, audio, and characters all worked together to make absurd situations and jokes land and feel like a natural part of the experience.
Why do you think games are well suited to comedy?
JM:
I think the whole "choose your own adventure" element that makes video game storytelling so satisfying is what makes them uniquely well suited for comedy as well. I just played the first Divinity: Original Sin game, and there's an optional quest where you're trying to reconnect a disembodied head with its body. Carrying the head around was funny, but there was nothing like the feeling of coming across a headless body and being like, "Oh yes, this is it!"
To share an example from Send In The Clown, the birthday girl's brother Tad tells you that their dad paid him $20 to stay in the garage during the party; however, if you had explored before that conversation and seen that the dad's most recent web search was "how much money to pay boy to behave," Tad will also say, "I don't know how my dad knew it, but $20 was exactly the right amount." It's that sort of customised-per-player writing that you just can't get in any other medium.
What's your reasoning for making a short game?
JM:
It's all about respecting the player's time. I love meaty JRPGs but simply don't have the time to play many of them. Part of the challenge and fun of making Send In The Clown was taking all of the elements of those JRPGs, like levelling up and building a party and making meaningful choices, and condensing them into a single, one-hour-ish comedy experience. It's basically the game we wish existed.
Nick Park  |
Image credit:
Mad Herons
NP:
We wanted to give players the best version of all of our stupid ideas and gags, and then let them go enjoy something else. Not everything has to be an epic. Bring back the 90-minute action blockbuster.
You talked about bootstrapping the studio – have you tried to raise funding? If so, how did it go? And how do you plan to pay for the development of the game?
NP:
As a studio we're focused on sustainability. We want to be able to keep working as a small team making games we're proud of, sharing profits with our collaborators, and not chasing rapid growth or betting the business on a single title. That pretty much ruled out the idea of venture capital or angel investors.
We did spend some time reaching out to publishers for Send In The Clown, but we were primarily looking for help with marketing expertise and promotional budgets, not funding development of the game itself. We got some really useful feedback during that process, but ultimately we didn't find a good match. Being first-time devs without an existing audience makes us a risky investment, and we were close enough to our release date when we started these conversations that we didn't line up with the standard contracts and schedules publishers operate on. That meant some folks who might have been willing to take those risks didn't have the bandwidth to jump in with us.
Luckily we're in a good position to self-fund development, and have been doing our best to learn how to market a game at the same time. Coming to game development after decades in other careers puts us in a fortunate position to be able to draw from savings and other investments to b
